title: Vestibular Disorders: BPPV and Vestibular Hypofunction
case: Presentation (from the chapter): Onset: Episodes triggered by position (lying down, rolling, looking up): Sudden continuous vertigo for days: Sudden. Duration of each episode: Seconds (usually less than a minute): Continuous for days, then gradual improvement: Continuous. Other signs: None between episodes: Nausea, imbalance; hearing normal in neuritis: Other neurological signs, severe imbalance, new headache

differentials.name: Vestibular neuritis
differentials.key: Days of vertigo, positive head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus

differentials.name: Ménière disease
differentials.key: Episodes lasting hours with hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness

differentials.name: Posterior circulation stroke
differentials.key: Neurological signs, severe imbalance, HINTS central

differentials.name: Cervicogenic dizziness
differentials.key: Neck pain linked to dizziness, diagnosis of exclusion

qa: What nystagmus suggests right posterior canal BPPV on Dix-Hallpike? Up-beating torsional nystagmus with the top of the eye beating toward the right (lower) ear, short latency, lasting under a minute.
Why is a positive head impulse test reassuring in acute vertigo? It points to a peripheral vestibular cause rather than central.
What exercise trains the VOR? Gaze stabilisation (VOR x1).
Dizziness lasting hours with tinnitus and hearing loss? Ménière disease: ENT referral.
When do you call emergency services? Vertigo with any central neurological sign or new severe headache.

fields.Purpose: Provoke vertigo and nystagmus from posterior canal BPPV
fields.Patient position: Long sitting on the couch, positioned so that the head will extend over the end when lying
fields.Therapist position: Standing beside or behind the head
fields.Action: Turn the head 45 degrees toward the tested side; quickly lay the patient back so the head is about 20 to 30 degrees below horizontal, keeping the rotation; watch the eyes for up to 30 to 60 seconds
fields.Positive: Vertigo with up-beating, torsional nystagmus (top of the eye beating toward the lower ear), starting after a short delay and fading within about a minute
fields.Next step: If positive, treat with the Epley manoeuvre for that side
fields.Caution: Check neck range and vascular screening; use a modified side-lying test if the neck cannot extend

redFlags.Finding: Vertigo with double vision, dysarthria, dysphagia, numbness, weakness, unable to stand or walk
New severe headache or neck pain with vertigo
Down-beating or pure vertical nystagmus without positional pattern
Positional vertigo that does not respond to several correct manoeuvres

manualNotes: Start as for the right Dix-Hallpike: head turned 45 degrees right, lie back with the head extended. Hold 30 to 60 seconds or until nystagmus stops.
Turn the head 90 degrees to the left (now 45 degrees left), keeping extension. Hold 30 to 60 seconds.
Roll the patient onto the left side, turning the head a further 90 degrees so the face points toward the floor. Hold 30 to 60 seconds.
Bring the patient up to sitting with the head still turned left and chin slightly tucked.
Re-test after a few minutes or at the next visit. Repeat if still positive.
Post-manoeuvre restrictions are generally not necessary [Ref – to verify].
Horizontal canal BPPV is treated with roll manoeuvres (for example barbecue roll) instead.

exercise.Steps: Look at a letter on a card at arm's length; move head side to side while keeping it in focus
exercise.Progress: Faster speed, busy background, standing, walking

exercise.Steps: Repeat movements that provoke mild dizziness
exercise.Starting dose: A few repetitions, several times daily

exercise.Steps: Feet together, tandem, eyes closed, foam
exercise.Progress: Dynamic tasks, head turns while walking

exerciseNotes: Symptom rule: mild, short-lived dizziness during exercises is expected and needed; dizziness lasting hours means reduce dose.
modalityNotes: Medications that suppress the vestibular system (for example some antiemetics and sedatives) may help in the first days but can slow adaptation if used long-term [Ref – to verify]. Coordinate with the doctor.
